articles.title: Nine Aeotec devices earn Home Assistant certification
articles.dek: Tested sensors, alarms and a switch come with a commitment to long-term support.
body: Eight Z-Wave products and the Zigbee Pico Switch have passed the Works with Home Assistant program’s checks for local operation and privacy. Aeotec commits to continued support and firmware updates for the listed devices, which include leak and door sensors alongside a siren.

Five of the certified products support Z-Wave Long Range. They need a compatible adapter, such as Connect ZWA-2, to use that direct-to-adapter connection; an older adapter still runs them as ordinary Z-Wave devices. The announcement lists US and European availability.

Jacqueline Ajayi’s announcement explains that certification covers the listed models rather than every device from the brand. Equipment outside the list can still work with Home Assistant; it may simply not have undergone the program’s testing.

articles.title: Local control for Pioneer WT air conditioners
articles.dek: Compatible WT modules can run ESPHome, with the handheld remote’s changes reflected in the controls.
body: A mini split that previously depended on Tuya’s service can instead exchange commands directly with an ESPHome device. The new Pioneer WT component talks over the indoor unit’s wired serial connection, using either a replacement board or compatible original hardware running custom firmware.

Mode, temperature, fan speed, vertical swing and an economy preset join optional controls for the display and beep. Reported state comes from the air conditioner itself, so a command is not mistaken for a completed change.

Martin Klingensmith tested one Pioneer WT unit with an ESP8266 board and with its original WBR3 module. Related serial-port support makes the original module usable without a workaround. Horizontal swing is not supported, and testing one unit does not establish compatibility with every Pioneer or TCL model.

articles.title: Bring Sony TVs and NAD hi-fi into your automations
articles.dek: Both connections use an infrared emitter; the audio integration also covers CD players and cassette decks.
body: A television or amplifier does not need its own network connection to receive commands from Home Assistant. Two new integrations send the infrared signals used by compatible Sony TVs and NAD audio equipment through an emitter already configured in the home.

Sony TV controls cover power, volume, mute and channel changes. NAD receivers and amplifiers add source and listening-mode selection; compatible CD players receive playback and track controls, while cassette decks support play, pause and stop. NAD receivers and amplifiers must use infrared channel 0.

The NAD integration assumes state from the commands it sends rather than confirming what the equipment did. CD and cassette controls do not include power. Gord makes a first contribution to Home Assistant Core with the Sony integration, alongside rrooggiieerr’s NAD work.

articles.title: Playback settings move into one place
articles.dek: Library, network and diagnostic options also get clearer homes, replacing scattered technical modules.
body: Changing crossfade, volume normalization or what happens when you press Play no longer means searching three separate System modules. A Playback page under Players brings those defaults together with autoplay, volume steps and announcements.

Music sources holds the library’s locations, genres and source preferences, while Metadata sources holds language, online lookups and artwork settings. System becomes a starting point for Network, Background tasks and Diagnostics; all module log levels sit together on Diagnostics.

The Players page separates speakers, lights, screens and audio inputs into their own groups. These are changes to where existing controls live; ordinary members still see only their own music sources, without the new library-settings links.

articles.title: One button can distinguish four kinds of press
articles.dek: Compatible event-based controls gain double, triple and quadruple choices, plus a condition for a continuing hold.
body: A single press can keep its existing action while a double press triggers something different. Home Assistant’s button trigger adds a press-count selector, with single through quadruple choices in the interface and higher counts available in YAML.
The device must report multiple presses itself; the trigger does not turn several separate clicks into a double press. Ordinary software buttons retain single-press behavior.

Abílio Costa also adds a condition that checks whether a button is still held. It needs separate start and end reports, so devices that only report a hold after release do not qualify. A thirty-second timeout prevents a missed release from leaving the condition true indefinitely.

pullRequests.title: Add multi press support to button.pressed trigger

articles.title: Duplicate tracks become one library entry
articles.dek: A shared recording identity is not enough: track length and the usual matching checks must agree.
body: A song kept from both Spotify and Tidal, or from a local file and a streaming service, can remain as two library entries even after both have been identified. Music Assistant uses the MusicBrainz catalogue’s recording identifiers to bring matching entries together.

The durations must be close and the normal track-matching checks must agree. A track carrying a second recording identity is left separate. The check runs when album tracks are matched, MusicBrainz is queried or an audio-fingerprint lookup supplies identifiers.

pullRequests.title: Merge library tracks of one MusicBrainz recording

articles.title: Read the warning before starting an update
articles.dek: Integrations can supply translated notices separately from their regular release notes.
body: A caution against cutting power should not be buried in a long list of changes. Home Assistant’s update dialog displays notices supplied by an integration above the release notes, with an alert style matching their severity.

Jan-Philipp Benecke connects the display to the new backend message format. The change provides a place for integrations to explain precautions; it does not invent warnings for every update. The accompanying screenshot demonstrates the layout with sample messages.

articles.title: Sleepy sensors spend less time waiting to report
articles.dek: A startup delay disappears for devices using MQTT; retries after a genuine connection failure keep their pause.
body: A battery-powered sensor can have Wi-Fi ready yet spend most of its waking time waiting to send a reading. ESPHome starts its first MQTT connection attempt as soon as the network is ready, instead of treating the early lack of a network like a failed attempt and waiting until five seconds after boot. MQTT is a messaging system commonly used to pass sensor readings.

Leandro’s first ESPHome contribution was tested on a BK7231N board sleeping for eight seconds between reports, with a precomputed Wi-Fi key and the message server supplied by address. Connections previously took about 5.1 seconds after boot; with the correction, seven of eight starts took about 0.8–1.5 seconds, and one took 3.5 seconds.

pullRequests.title: [mqtt] Connect as soon as the network is up, not 5 s after boot

articles.title: Some older Squeezebox players lose synchronized grouping
articles.dek: Squeezebox-only groups switch to Sendspin; solo playback and groups with separate streams retain their existing paths.
body: The original Squeezebox from 2003 and players supplied through Logitech Media Server bridge tools cannot join synchronized groups under the new arrangement: they lack the required Sendspin output. Compatible Squeezebox and squeezelite speakers use that connection even when the group contains no other kind of player.

Adding or removing a member no longer restarts the music on the remaining speakers. Solo playback keeps its existing path, as do universal groups, where each member plays a separate stream. The new restriction changes the Squeezebox-only grouping that remained untouched in the November 16 coverage.

pullRequests.title: Play every group of Squeezebox and squeezelite speakers through Sendspin

articles.title: A dried leak probe stops reporting a flood
articles.dek: The Ecolink FLF-ZWAVE5 clears its alert from the device’s own dry signal, rather than a timer.
body: A wet probe could leave the default water-leak entity in Home Assistant stuck on long after it dried. The Ecolink sensor sends a different notification for dry conditions, which Z-Wave JS previously interpreted without clearing the earlier alarm.

@twagner12’s first contribution to Z-Wave JS maps that signal to the end of the leak alert. This avoids a timed reset that could conceal water still present. The correction is supported by a recorded wet-to-dry exchange; the contributor has not yet tested the changed mapping on the device.

pullRequests.title: fix(config): idle water leak notification on Ecolink FLF-ZWAVE5 when the probe dries

articles.title: Dim orange LEDs stop turning yellow
articles.dek: Addressable strips preserve the dominant colour while retaining the safeguard against going completely dark.
body: An orange-red light at a few percent brightness could become yellow because its red and green channels were both rounded up to the same tiny value. ESPHome instead considers the whole pixel, allowing a weak colour channel to drop to zero while the stronger one remains lit.

Keith Burzinski checked the change on a twelve-LED SK6812 RGBW ring. Dim white stays white, while a very dim orange resolves toward red instead of yellow; the correction does not claim perfect colour reproduction below the strip’s available brightness steps.

pullRequests.title: [light] Keep the colour of a dim addressable pixel

articles.title: Custom AUX-2 firmware regains missing audio and Zigbee features
articles.dek: The adopted configuration requires ESPHome 2026.11.0 and restores 24-bit Sendspin audio.
body: Owners taking control of a Connect AUX-2 no longer need the reduced configuration introduced to keep custom firmware building with an older stable ESPHome release. The imported configuration includes both 24-bit Sendspin playback and the Zigbee proxy feature that handles time-sensitive acknowledgements locally.
Keith Burzinski compiled the factory and adopted configurations with ESPHome 2026.11.0. This restores the capabilities left out of custom builds on November 10; factory firmware already had them.

articles.title: Keep a wall switch from changing the device
articles.dek: An input-lock control covers supported Shelly switches and shutters from generation two onward.
body: A physical input can be ignored while an automation keeps control of the connected equipment. The new Home Assistant switch changes the input-lock setting on supported Shelly switch and cover components.
Yuval Weiss tested a Shelly 1PM Mini Gen3 and a Plus 2PM configured for a shutter. The new control appears by default in Home Assistant; the physical input does not start locked.

articles.title: Setup descriptions stop loading tracking images
articles.dek: Images in biographies and programme notes remain; the restriction applies to text supplied by providers.
body: A hidden image in a provider’s description could contact an outside server when someone opened its settings. Music Assistant removes remote images and other media from provider-written labels, alerts, setup text, errors, task reports and Marketplace credits.
Setup illustrations still work when embedded in the data sent by the provider. Built-in providers already use that approach, so their setup appearance stays the same.

pullRequests.title: Load no remote images from provider text

articles.title: A paired device brings its audio input with it
articles.dek: The separate Sendspin Source plugin is removed; automatic playback settings stay on the device.
body: A turntable, line-in or microphone attached to a Sendspin device becomes a Music Assistant audio source as soon as that device is paired. There is no additional source plugin to find and enable.
Upgrades remove the old plugin’s stored settings. Line-in autostart and the per-device controls remain on the Sendspin device itself.

articles.title: A visible exit for the full-screen player
articles.dek: Wall tablets avoid a swipe that reloads the page; keyboard and screen-reader users gain the same labelled control.
body: Fully Kiosk Browser can intercept the downward swipe meant to close Music Assistant’s player and reload the page instead. The close chevron stays visible on phones and tablets, giving those screens a direct way back.
Piero reproduced the problem with pull-to-refresh enabled in an Android emulator at tablet and phone sizes, then checked the correction on a real phone.

pullRequests.title: Always show the close chevron on the fullscreen player

articles.title: Old SmartThings switches and sensors need replacement
articles.dek: Media-player and water-heater controls take over from entities deprecated since 2025.
body: Dashboards, templates and automations still pointing to the older entities need to use their replacements. Appliance switches give way to binary status sensors, while media-player switches and separate source, repeat, shuffle, playback and volume sensors give way to the media-player entity.

For heat pumps with domestic hot water, the water-heater entity replaces the old switch and temperature or cooling-setpoint sensors. This removes the deprecated copies; it does not remove the supported equipment from Home Assistant.

pullRequests.title: Remove deprecated entities from SmartThings

roadmapUpdates.title: Marketplace redesign focuses on discovery
roadmapUpdates.summary: A revised Home Assistant proposal in Shaping would combine Discover and Browse, with paths by content type or goal. Changes to individual item pages and the Installed page are now outside its scope; keeping the table view for power users remains an open question.
